topic: Why Spain Is Stranger Than You Think (Perejil Island war of 2002)
hook: Your holiday in Spain can put you in Africa, and a goat island there once nearly started a war.
title: Why Spain Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
Spain keeps cities in Africa, a town inside France, and a clock that follows the wrong country. In 2002 it even sent troops to a bare rock called Perejil Island and nearly went to war with Morocco. Here are six true facts about Spain's time, borders and map that sound fake but are real.

#Spain #Geography #StrangeFacts

scenes.narration: Your holiday in Spain can put you in Africa, and a goat island there once nearly started a war.
scenes.headline: Spain Is In Africa

scenes.narration: That rock is real, it is bare, and in 2002 two countries almost went to war over it.
scenes.headline: A War Over A Rock

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will see the smallest war that never quite happened.
scenes.headline: The Tiny Near-War

scenes.narration: But first, six facts that make Spain stranger than almost any country in Europe.
scenes.headline: 6 Strange Facts

scenes.narration: Some are on the map, some are on your watch, and one is right on an airport runway.
scenes.headline: Map, Watch, Runway

scenes.narration: Let us start with the clock on your wrist, because Spain is living in the wrong time.
scenes.headline: The Wrong Time

scenes.narration: Fact one: Spain is on the wrong time zone, and it has been that way for over eighty years.
scenes.headline: Spain's Wrong Clock

scenes.narration: Look at a globe. Madrid sits roughly in line with London and Lisbon, yet its clocks follow Berlin and Paris.
scenes.headline: In Line With London

scenes.narration: In 1940, Spain's ruler Franco moved the clocks forward one hour, to match Nazi Germany.
scenes.headline: Franco Moved The Clocks

scenes.narration: When the war ended, Spain never changed the clocks back, and it still uses that same time today.
scenes.headline: Never Changed Back

scenes.narration: So in summer, the sun in Madrid can set after nine thirty at night.
scenes.headline: Sunset After 9:30

scenes.narration: That is one reason a Spanish dinner often starts at nine or even ten at night.
scenes.headline: Dinner At Ten

scenes.narration: Shops close for a long afternoon break, and the streets come alive again late in the evening.
scenes.headline: The Long Break

scenes.narration: Even prime-time television starts late, close to ten at night, so the whole country lives a few hours behind its clock.
scenes.headline: Late-Night Prime Time

scenes.narration: People in Spain keep debating whether to switch to London time and finally fix it.
scenes.headline: Switch To London Time?

scenes.narration: Imagine eating dinner at ten at night and calling it normal. In Spain, that is just a Tuesday.
scenes.headline: Just A Tuesday

scenes.narration: Fact two: a Spanish town is stuck inside France, with French land on every single side.
scenes.headline: Spain Inside France

scenes.narration: It is called Llívia, and it sits in the Pyrenees mountains, a short drive from the Spanish border.
scenes.headline: Llívia

scenes.narration: In 1659, Spain and France signed a treaty, and Spain handed over a whole set of villages.
scenes.headline: The 1659 Treaty

scenes.narration: But Llívia was officially a town, not a village, so Spain kept it. One word saved it.
scenes.headline: Town, Not Village

scenes.narration: Today it is a Spanish exclave, a small town with Spanish flags flying in the middle of France.
scenes.headline: A Spanish Exclave

scenes.narration: A short road through French land links it to Spain, and that road is treated as neutral.
scenes.headline: The Neutral Road

scenes.narration: Drive it, and you leave Spain, pass through France without stopping, and arrive back in Spain.
scenes.headline: Spain, France, Spain

scenes.narration: Indian viewers may think of Dahagram, the Bangladeshi pocket inside India. Llívia is the same idea, in Europe.
scenes.headline: Like Dahagram

scenes.narration: Its old pharmacy is one of the oldest in Europe, and people visit just to see it.
scenes.headline: An Old Pharmacy

scenes.narration: The streets look like any Pyrenean town, with Spanish signs, Catalan voices and French hills all around.
scenes.headline: Catalan In France

scenes.narration: One small word in a treaty, written over three hundred years ago, still draws this border today.
scenes.headline: 300 Years Later

scenes.narration: But Spain has an even stranger place, and this one has a road that crosses an airport runway.
scenes.headline: Next: A Runway Road

scenes.narration: Fact three: at Gibraltar, a normal road crosses the airport runway, and traffic stops for airplanes.
scenes.headline: Cars Stop For Planes

scenes.narration: Gibraltar is a British territory at Spain's southern tip, with a huge rock rising above the town.
scenes.headline: The Rock Of Gibraltar

scenes.narration: Spain claims it, Britain keeps it, and people walk between the two every day.
scenes.headline: Walk Between Countries

scenes.narration: Walk out of the border gate and you step straight onto the runway road, called Winston Churchill Avenue.
scenes.headline: Winston Churchill Avenue

scenes.narration: When a plane lands or takes off, the barriers drop, and cars, bikes and walkers all have to wait.
scenes.headline: Barriers Drop

scenes.narration: Then the plane rolls across the exact spot where you were standing a few seconds earlier.
scenes.headline: Plane On Your Road

scenes.narration: Planes come in with the huge rock rising behind them, which makes it a famous airport to watch.
scenes.headline: A Famous Airport

scenes.narration: The whole territory is smaller than a typical city district, yet it has its own government and its own police.
scenes.headline: Tiny But Self-Ruling

scenes.narration: If you like strange places and facts like these, subscribe, because there are plenty more coming.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: And now the land that really looks wrong on a map, because it sits in Africa and belongs to Spain.
scenes.headline: Spain On Africa's Coast

scenes.narration: Fact four: Spain has two cities on Africa's coast, Ceuta and Melilla, and both have land borders with Morocco.
scenes.headline: Ceuta And Melilla

scenes.narration: Both have been under Spanish rule for centuries, long before Morocco became an independent country.
scenes.headline: Spanish For Centuries

scenes.narration: They are the only places where the European Union has a land border with Africa.
scenes.headline: EU's Only African Border

scenes.narration: So a fence in Africa marks the edge of the EU, with Spanish police standing guard.
scenes.headline: A Fence In Africa

scenes.narration: People in Ceuta pay in euros, speak Spanish, and look out at Moroccan mountains from the beach.
scenes.headline: Euros In Africa

scenes.narration: Morocco says both cities should belong to it, while Spain says they are as Spanish as Madrid.
scenes.headline: Who Owns Them?

scenes.narration: India knows this story too. Goa stayed Portuguese until 1961, long after India's independence.
scenes.headline: Goa Until 1961

scenes.narration: Ceuta sits so close to Europe that you can see the coast of Spain across the water.
scenes.headline: Europe In Sight

scenes.narration: The Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 kilometres wide at its narrowest, so Africa really is that close.
scenes.headline: 14 km Apart

scenes.narration: Spain's reach into Africa does not stop there. Some of it sits even closer, out in the ocean.
scenes.headline: Next: Ocean Islands

scenes.narration: Fact five: the Canary Islands are Spanish, but they sit off the coast of Africa, not Europe.
scenes.headline: The Canary Islands

scenes.narration: From Fuerteventura, Morocco is far closer than mainland Spain, which is more than a thousand kilometres away.
scenes.headline: Closer To Morocco

scenes.narration: They are part of Spain and the EU, so tourists pay in euros while looking toward the Sahara.
scenes.headline: Euros Near The Sahara

scenes.narration: The islands even have their own time zone, one hour behind mainland Spain.
scenes.headline: A Separate Time Zone

scenes.narration: So you can take a flight within Spain and have your watch go back an hour.
scenes.headline: Same Country, New Time

scenes.narration: On Tenerife stands Mount Teide, the highest mountain in all of Spain, and it is a volcano.
scenes.headline: Mount Teide

scenes.narration: In winter, snow falls on its top, while the beaches below stay warm.
scenes.headline: Snow Above, Sun Below

scenes.narration: At times, sand blows in from the Sahara and turns the sky orange and hazy.
scenes.headline: Sahara Sand In The Sky

scenes.narration: Now the story I promised: a rock so small that it nearly caused a war between two countries.
scenes.headline: The Goat-Island Crisis

scenes.narration: Fact six: Perejil Island, a bare rock just off Morocco's coast, brought Spain and Morocco close to war.
scenes.headline: Perejil Island

scenes.narration: Perejil means parsley in Spanish. Morocco calls it Leila, and both countries say it is theirs.
scenes.headline: Parsley Or Leila?

scenes.narration: It has no houses and no people. The island is known mostly for goats.
scenes.headline: Just A Goat Rock

scenes.narration: It sits only a few hundred metres from the Moroccan coast, not far from the Spanish city of Ceuta.
scenes.headline: Metres From Morocco

scenes.narration: For decades, neither country kept a flag or a soldier on it. It was simply nobody's rock.
scenes.headline: Nobody's Rock

scenes.narration: Then, on the eleventh of July 2002, a small group of Moroccan soldiers landed, raised a flag and set up camp.
scenes.headline: Soldiers Land

scenes.narration: Morocco said it was watching for smugglers and illegal migrants. Spain heard something very different.
scenes.headline: Two Stories

scenes.narration: Spain said the move broke the old understanding that nobody would occupy the rock, and asked Morocco to leave.
scenes.headline: Spain Says Leave

scenes.narration: The European Union backed Spain, while the Arab League backed Morocco, and Morocco still did not move.
scenes.headline: The World Picks Sides

scenes.narration: On the seventeenth of July, Spanish helicopters and navy ships came in at dawn.
scenes.headline: Dawn Raid

scenes.narration: Spanish troops landed, took the handful of Moroccan soldiers, and raised a Spanish flag on the rock.
scenes.headline: Spanish Flag Raised

scenes.narration: No one was killed. The soldiers were flown to Ceuta and handed back to Morocco.
scenes.headline: Nobody Was Killed

scenes.narration: Morocco was furious, and for a few days it looked like two countries might really start fighting.
scenes.headline: On The Edge

scenes.narration: Then the American Secretary of State, Colin Powell, phoned both sides and helped them agree on a deal.
scenes.headline: Colin Powell Steps In

scenes.narration: The deal was simple: go back to how things were before the eleventh of July.
scenes.headline: Back To Before

scenes.narration: Spain took its troops out, the Spanish flag came down, and the island went back to being empty.
scenes.headline: Empty Again

scenes.narration: Even the name stays disputed: Perejil to Spain, Leila to Morocco, and Tura in Arabic.
scenes.headline: Three Names, One Rock

scenes.narration: Today the dispute is still unresolved. Both claims remain, and the rock is still bare.
scenes.headline: Still Unresolved

scenes.narration: Many people joked about a war over parsley, but soldiers and warships on both sides were really there.
scenes.headline: A War Over Parsley

scenes.narration: So yes, your holiday in Spain can put you in Africa, and a goat island really did nearly start a war.
scenes.headline: Spain Is Stranger

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: the city that sits on two continents at once.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow: Two Continents
